title: Bias-Proof Backtesting Framework
context:
Backtesting is where quant careers are made and quietly destroyed: a framework with a look-ahead bug turns noise into a beautiful equity curve, and the loss appears only with live money. Most in-house frameworks are built by juniors, audited by nobody, and trusted by everybody — which is why bias prevention is designed in, not tested in.

This project asks you to build a small event-driven backtester whose defining feature is *honesty*: signals execute at a defensible price with real costs, the walk-forward harness resists overfitting, and a built-in self-test proves that a deliberately cheating strategy is caught. The framework is deliberately minimal — one instrument, daily bars — so the hard parts (sequencing, accounting, bias guards) are visible instead of buried under data plumbing.
problem:
Build an event-driven backtesting framework for daily-bar strategies on a single instrument:

- **Data layer**: loads OHLCV CSV, verifies strictly chronological unique dates, and exposes to strategies only a *view capped at the current bar* — reaching beyond it must be impossible by construction (and provable).
- **Strategy interface**: `on_bar(bar, position) -> target_weight`; the engine converts target weights to orders on the *next* bar's open (or same-bar close — pick one, document it, and state the bias implication).
- **Execution**: configurable commission (bps with a minimum fee) and slippage (half-spread plus a square-root market-impact term); fills update cash and position; equity marked at close.
- **Accounting**: cash conservation must hold exactly; the engine asserts it every bar.
- **Walk-forward**: split history into consecutive train/validation windows; a parameter grid is optimised on train, evaluated untouched on validation; aggregated out-of-sample results reported next to in-sample ones.
- **Look-ahead self-test**: a shipping test containing a 'cheating' strategy (sneaks future data through any hole it can find) that must raise, be blocked, or produce a flagged difference — the test documents exactly what the guard catches.
- **Report**: total return, CAGR, annualised vol, Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover and total cost drag; equity and drawdown CSVs; all deterministic.
requirements: Deterministic, reproducible runs: same input produces byte-identical reports; any random element takes a seed from config.

Data guard: the strategy-visible data view implements an index cap so that any access past the current bar raises `LookaheadError`; the self-test strategy attempts at least two evasion routes (e.g. closure capture, length probing) and is caught.

Execution semantics explicitly chosen and documented: signal at close t, fill at open t+1 (or same-bar close with a stated bias warning); costs applied on every fill with a worked example in the docs.
Cost model: commission in bps with a minimum fee, plus slippage = half-spread + k * sqrt(order_size / ADV); parameters from config; a zero-cost mode must exactly reproduce a frictionless baseline.
Accounting invariants asserted every bar: shorting rules honoured, cash + position * price == equity, no negative holdings unless shorting is enabled.
Walk-forward runner: configurable window count/length; selection metric from config; aggregated out-of-sample equity and a per-window table in the report.
Performance report metrics computed from the equity curve: CAGR, vol, Sharpe, max DD, turnover, cost drag — each with a unit test on a synthetic curve.

designGuidance.md: The one-bar delay is the cheapest honest design: a strategy sees the close of bar $t$, expresses a target weight, and the engine fills at the open of bar $t+1$. Filling a close-$t$ signal at the close of bar $t$ assumes you traded at the exact print you saw — a bias that inflates momentum strategies. If you must fill same-bar, you owe the reader an explicit warning and a slippage model that plausibly covers it.

designGuidance.code:
for i, bar in enumerate(bars):
    view = DataWindow(bars, i)              # capped: view[i+1:] raises
    signal = strategy.on_bar(view.current(), engine.position)
    if i + 1 < len(bars):                   # engine-side lookahead is fine;
        engine.execute(signal.target_weight, fill_price=bars[i + 1].open)
    engine.mark_to_market(bar.close)
    assert engine.equity == engine.cash + engine.position * bar.close
designGuidance.caption: The engine may see the future internally; the strategy may not

designGuidance.title: The quiet look-aheads
designGuidance.md: Classic leaks: a rolling mean that includes the current bar and is then acted on as if known before the close; `pct_change` vs `shift` confusion; normalising by a statistic computed over the full sample (a *future* quantity); tuning parameters against full-sample optimisers. Each deserves a line in your bias checklist.

items: **Index probing**: `data[i + 1]` and requests for 'the last bar' when the true length would reveal the future — the view must not leak true length or future rows.
**Closure capture**: a strategy that stashes a full-length reference at construction — the guard must live in the view, not in the strategy's good manners.
**Ordering tricks**: reaching 'the bar after the last' via negative indices or iterators.
Document what the guard does *not* catch (e.g. survivorship issues, look-ahead inside indicator internals the view wraps) — honesty includes the limits.

designGuidance.title: Walk-forward beats a single split
designGuidance.md: A single train/test split can get lucky. Rolling walk-forward windows measure *stability* of the edge across regimes, and the gap between in-sample and out-of-sample Sharpe is your overfitting telemetry: report both, always.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Look-ahead guard design and demonstrable self-test catching planted cheats
Engine correctness: sequencing, fill semantics, accounting invariants asserted
Cost model realism and worked examples; zero-cost equivalence
Walk-forward methodology and honest in-sample/out-of-sample reporting
Performance metrics correctness with unit tests on synthetic curves
Documentation: bias checklist, semantics decisions, reproducibility

documentationRequirements: README.md: architecture, execution-semantics decision and its bias implication, run instructions for a demo strategy.
BIAS-CHECKLIST.md: every look-ahead vector the framework defends against, how the guard works, and known blind spots.
A worked cost example: one fill traced end-to-end from order to cash impact with real numbers.
Reproducibility note: seeds, determinism guarantees, golden-file testing.
extensionChallenges: Add multi-asset support with per-asset views and cross-sectional signal normalisation (rank-based weights).
Implement a vectorised backtester over the same config and reconcile results against the event-driven engine bar by bar — disagreements are bugs in one of them.
Add a simple regime filter (volatility targeting) and measure out-of-sample Sharpe stability across walk-forward windows.
